# Applications: Athlete Monitoring Analytics presented by Fusion Sport

Caveat: the captions for this talk are badly garbled, so only the general architecture (integrate sources, automate reports, tier access, visualize against a performance model) is usable. Treat details as unverified.

## Where this applies

- Inference: Automating the post-session Catapult-to-report step. The speaker described GPS data uploading automatically, with no double entry, and coach summary reports generating once processing finishes [03:05] [05:44]. At Baylor this maps to the OpenField export, cleaning and PDF step in the GPS SOP, with the target of zero manual touches between sync and the coach's inbox.
- Inference: Pulling VALD (ForceDecks, NordBord, DynaMo) and GPS output into one athlete view in Kitman Labs, as the talk pushed all sources into one hub that feeds back into a performance model [00:00] [01:01].
- Inference: A weekly screen-versus-position dashboard. The talk showed weekly musculoskeletal screening values (dorsiflexion named) plotted against position and team ranges, with outliers flagged and drill-down to injury history [04:38] [05:11]. This could become a one-page view of DynaMo or ForceDecks outliers by position group for Athletic Medicine.
- Inference: Role-based access tiers for dashboards. The talk raised different security levels for different audiences [06:48]. Baylor could define separate views for coaches, Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Kitman Labs is the cross-technology data store and visualization layer, separate from each vendor's own reporting tool. The talk agrees on the architecture (one integrated layer), though its tool names are garbled.
- Eric's baseline: Standardized weekly and monthly coach-facing reporting templates do not yet exist and are named as unfinished Phase 2 work. The talk extends this by showing automated, trigger-on-upload reports as the end state.
- Eric's baseline: Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance and staff attention, and should stop when insight no longer justifies it; daily wellness surveys were dropped after athletes gamed them. The talk includes wellness data in its summary reports [05:44] without addressing this, so it conflicts mildly with Eric's experience. The speaker's answer on coach buy-in (that mandating monitoring backfires, as best the garbled captions show) [08:51] fits Eric's operations-first view.

## What would have to be true

- A working API or export path from each source system into Kitman Labs, with an agreed athlete ID key.
- A defined performance model (the talk's starting point [00:00]) so dashboards show gaps against something, not just values.
- Agreement from Athletic Medicine on which injury fields (for example injuries within seven days [04:07]) may appear on a coach-facing display.

## Do not apply when

- The details are needed as fact: the captions are too garbled to confirm product names, the number of sports, or the access model.
- The talk is a vendor sponsor talk (Fusion Sport is in the title), so it shows capability, not outcomes. No evidence of injury or performance benefit was presented.
- Medical information would be shown on shared screens without a privacy rule. The talk mentions TVs in facilities and hubs for case conferences [03:36] [06:14].

## First step

List the manual touch points between a Catapult session ending and the coach report landing (sync, cleaning, tagging, export). Count them for one week of practices, then pick the single one that could be automated.

# Applications: Built to Outlast, Youth Athlete Development

## Where this applies

- Inference: Recruiting and intake profiling of incoming freshmen. The talk argues late specialization and multi-sport backgrounds go with fewer injuries and longer careers [09:56] [10:26]. Recording sport-history (years of single-sport focus) at intake could flag athletes who arrive with poor general movement competency, without implying any cutoff.
- Inference: Reading growth and maturity context in the youngest recruits. The speaker said different domains carry outsized influence at different times, such as biomechanics during rapid growth [18:15]. This could inform how cautiously a 17 or 18 year old early enrollee is progressed.
- Inference: Framing the load-recovery conversation with coaches using the speaker's load and recovery continuum, where overload without enough recovery erodes capacity [04:46] [05:17].
- Inference: Combining numeric data with subjective context in athlete review meetings. The talk calls the non-quantifiable inputs "fuzzy data" and says they should be considered alongside measured data [16:44] [21:18].

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before advanced work, since many incoming athletes have high sport skill but poor general movement competency. The talk agrees (foundational strength and movement skill before sport skill) [08:22] [08:53].
- Eric's baseline: Injury risk is reduced, not eliminated, and progressions are kept smooth; bodyweight competency is treated as an injury-risk marker. The talk agrees on the foundation point and extends it to a youth pipeline view. The speaker also notes traumatic injuries are inherent to sport [26:33].
- Eric's baseline: Preparedness is distinguished from readiness. The talk's per-athlete recovery answer (varies by athlete and activity, days after a game) [23:51] is consistent with this, though it does not use those terms.
- Eric's baseline: The Applied Performance playbook stresses collaboration with Athletic Medicine. The speaker is a sports medicine physician and frames health and performance as one continuum [00:35], which agrees.

## What would have to be true

- The youth findings (specialization, injury) would need to be checked against Baylor's own incoming-athlete history; the talk presented no numbers for them in the captions.
- Intake sport-history data would need to be recorded consistently by Athletic Performance and Athletic Medicine.
- A named person would need to own the "fuzzy data" notes so they are not lost.

## Do not apply when

- Deciding on individual college athletes: the talk is about youth athletes and a population view, and gives no thresholds.
- Treating it as evidence for a Baylor protocol. The complex-systems idea is the speaker's own hypothesis [17:15], not tested results, and the speaker admits we do not really know what drives elite performance [14:40].
- Interpreting the NBA multi-sport comment [10:26] as causal. It was a brief statement without a sample size.

## First step

Add one optional field to the new-athlete intake form for sport history (sports played and ages at which the athlete focused on one). Review it after one recruiting class before using it for any decision.

# Applications: Performance Optimization Strategies that Helped Win a Championship

## Where this applies

- Inference: An availability objective for key players. The West Coast Eagles tracked how many of their top 10 players played each week and tied it to winning rate [12:49]. A football equivalent would be a weekly count of starters and key rotation players available, built from PFF grades and the Athletic Medicine report, tracked against the team's own results over several seasons.
- Inference: A chronic-load floor for the preseason and the break after the season. The speaker kept a rolling four-week average, warned that a two-week break leaves players exposed on return [17:58], and said players must train in off periods [18:30]. At Baylor this maps to GPS-derived load for the weeks before fall camp and after winter break.
- Inference: A "hardest period" benchmark from GPS. The Eagles took the hardest rolling 15 minutes for their team over five years and built drills to match or beat it [19:33] [20:06]. For football this would be the most demanding drive or period per position group from OpenField, used as a practice target.
- Inference: A one-page objectives and key results sheet for Applied Performance, using the speaker's vision, mission, objectives, strategies and tactics layout with a measurable key result per objective [10:45] [11:46], such as the less-than-15%-recurrent-injuries example.

## Eric's baseline

- Eric's baseline: No formal injury-risk model (ACWR or similar) is attributed to him in the corpus; progressions are kept smooth and abrupt changes are seen as an injury-risk driver. The talk extends this with a rolling-average and colored risk-band approach (two times and three to five times risk) [17:27], which is the speaker's own club view with no source given.
- Eric's baseline: Recovery has to be earned by training hard, and over-protective "culture of fear" monitoring leaves athletes under-prepared. The talk agrees: it wants maximal training and warns about dropping chronic load [18:30].
- Eric's baseline: Data collection must justify its cost, simple and consistent beats exhaustive, and monitoring should not overwhelm coaches. The talk agrees: simple but not simpler, do not blindside coaches with data [22:10].
- Eric's baseline: Conditioning means meeting the sport's energy demands, and 75 to 90 percent effort is avoided as "no man's land" for training. The talk's drills exceed the hardest-ever running [20:38], which differs in framing (a work-density benchmark, not an effort-zone rule). Compatible, not a direct conflict.
- Eric's baseline: Applied Performance supports Athletics Performance and Athletic Medicine. The talk's single shared plan aligning staff with coaches [21:39] agrees on collaboration.

## What would have to be true

- Several seasons of consistent GPS and availability data for football, with a stable definition of "top players" (the Eagles used an official provider's player scores [14:23]).
- A football-specific link between availability and results. The 80% and two-thirds win figures are one club's AFL data, and the football relationship would need testing on Baylor's own seasons.
- Chronic-load windows need regular exposure, which in college football depends on NCAA practice limits, not just choices.

## Do not apply when

- Treating one club's risk bands (two times, three to five times) as validated for football; the speaker gave no source or sample.
- Using the findings with small samples: 25 games and one team's season [14:53].
- Copying the AFL context, where the field is 170 by 130 m and games involve distances of 15 to 16 km for a midfielder [18:30] [20:06]. Football play structure is different.
- The speaker himself said modeling is limited because the game is chaotic and fields and conditions vary [23:47].

## First step

Pull the last two seasons of weekly team GPS totals, compute a rolling four-week average, and plot it with the weeks after winter break marked. No decision attached; look only at how far it dipped.

# SSAC18: Athlete Monitoring Analytics presented by Fusion Sport

## Summary

A short vendor-sponsored talk (title names Fusion Sport) on integrating the data streams a university athletic program collects, so that decisions are centralized and tied to a shared performance model. The speaker describes pushing data from a programming tool, GPS units and an electronic medical record into one system without double entry, then showing it back to coaches, athletes and medical staff as dashboards, automatic reports and role-based reports. The captions are heavily garbled, so details are uncertain and no outcome evidence is presented. The talk reads as a capability demonstration for a product, not a study.

## Key claims

- The aim is to use data for corrective purposes with centralized decision-making, which first requires agreeing on what is monitored and defining a performance model everyone understands [00:00].
- The program aggregates many technologies across training, recovery, practice and injury identification and feeds the data back into that model [01:01].
- A strength-programming tool (captions: "Bridge Athletic") connects through an API so athlete data entered on gym iPads flows into the system without further handling [01:32] [02:03] [02:34].
- GPS units used across several sports (captions name American football, soccer and volleyball) upload automatically, so no one enters data twice [02:34] [03:05].
- Injury data from an electronic medical record is visualized for coaches and medical staff on phones, tablets, PCs and facility TVs, including injuries within seven days [03:36] [04:07].
- Weekly musculoskeletal screening (dorsiflexion is named) is shown against position and team ranges, with outliers flagged and drill-down to injury history [04:38] [05:11].
- Reports for coaches are generated automatically after GPS data processes, and wellness and injury information is summarized by group [05:44] [06:14].
- A Microsoft visualization tool (caption spelling garbled) provides access at different security levels, including season summaries, availability, cross-team comparison and individual athlete progress [06:48] [07:19].

## Numbers and definitions

- Seven days: injury highlighting window ("injuries within seven days") [04:07]. Captions are garbled around this.
- "90 sport" and "two years in the process" appear in the answer on rollout [09:23]. Caption likely garbled; do not rely on either figure.
- No performance or injury outcome numbers are given.

## Methods and frameworks named

- A performance model used to identify discrepancies in athlete development and decide what to test [00:00] [00:30].
- Integration by API and automatic upload from three source types: programming tool, GPS, electronic medical record [01:32] to [03:36].
- Dashboards and hubs for individual case conferences covering items such as hydration, body composition and past injuries [06:14].

## Limits and open questions

- Captions are too garbled to confirm product names, the sport list, or the access-control description.
- Speaker is not named in the captions. The institution is described only as a university.
- Commercial context: the talk is presented by Fusion Sport. No evidence of benefit to athletes or outcomes was shown.
- Does not address data quality, athlete privacy for medical data on shared displays, or the cost of integration.

## Q&A

- Do athletes use the data to help recovery? Answer (partly garbled): medical staff and coaches inform the athletes, and it becomes a conversation and an intervention [08:21].
- Is coach buy-in mandatory? Answer (garbled): mandating it would be the fastest way to ensure no one does it; some coaches are more interested than others, and the system takes their own inputs and makes them meaningful to them [08:51] [09:23].

# SSAC19: Built to Outlast: Youth Athlete Development for Performance and Durability

## Summary

A sports medicine physician argues that injury and performance sit on one health continuum and that youth athletes should be developed with a complex-systems view, not by studying single factors. She describes adolescence as a period of peak growth and change, falling and unequal sports participation, and a booming youth sports market that pushes early specialization, overload and under-built movement foundations. Her recommendation is "smart specialization": multi-sport, athlete-centered, skill-driven activity with foundational strength and movement first. The talk is a conceptual argument with few data points, and the complex-systems framework is her stated hypothesis.

## Key claims

- Injury and performance states lie on the same health continuum, and the goal is to keep athletes on the healthy, adaptive side [00:35] [01:39] [02:09].
- Health should be assessed across four domains: physiologic, biomechanic, behavioral and mental, and environmental [02:09].
- The transition into adolescence brings peak growth velocity and major brain and social change, so health determinants become performance determinants [02:42] [03:12] [03:45].
- Training load is system stress, and the aim is to raise capacity for it; youth athletes are often overloaded without enough recovery, which erodes capacity [04:15] [04:46] [05:17].
- Sports participation overall is falling, and the speaker ties access to socioeconomic status: lower-status athletes face sedentary-behavior risk, higher-status athletes face early specialization and injury risk [05:48] [06:18] [06:48].
- Youth athletes are over-scheduled, over-coached and spend less time on foundational strength and movement skills, which the speaker links to injury and attrition [08:22] [08:53] [09:26].
- Athletes who reach elite levels tend to specialize later, and highly specialized high school athletes are at higher injury risk [09:56]. Among NBA players, multi-sport athletes tended to miss fewer games, last longer and be less likely to be injured [10:26].
- The American development model has five stages; stage one, discover, learn and play, runs from age zero to twelve [10:57] [11:27].
- Studying loading, recovery and fueling one factor at a time misses their interactions; performance is a pattern emerging from relationships among determinants, whose influence changes over time [14:40] [16:13] [17:15] [17:45] [18:15].
- Because of this, models should be continuously reassessed, and the speaker holds that this approach yields more predictable outcomes [18:45] [19:48].
- Recommended approach is smart specialization: structured, supervised, multi-sport, athlete-centered, readiness- and skill-focused activity [20:48]. Practical steps include calibrating to physiologic and cognitive stage, mixing quantitative and "fuzzy" data, sport sampling, athlete engagement, and linking performance goals to health goals [21:18] [21:48].
- Future directions: cluster sports by shared physical demands, refine the language of training load, find protective or enhancing sport clusters, and focus on dissemination [22:18] [22:49].

## Numbers and definitions

- Youth sports market: twenty-two billion dollars worldwide, projected near sixty billion by 2024 [07:51].
- Stage one of the development model: ages 0 to 12; the model's activities are shown across ages 0 to 20 [11:27] [11:57].
- "Fuzzy data": elements that cannot easily be quantified but influence other parts of the system [16:44].
- Complex system: multifactorial web of related determinants that is iterative, recursive, self-organizing, decentralized and adaptive [16:44] [17:15].
- Training load: defined as system stress [04:15].
- Participation decline and the market projection are attributed to an Aspen Institute report and, for the market, no named source [05:48] [07:51].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Performance-health-disease continuum (credited to Dr. Fran O'Connor, military sports medicine) [01:39].
- Four-domain health assessment [02:09].
- Load and recovery continuum [04:46].
- American development model, five stages [10:57].
- Complex-systems approach with "fuzzy data" [16:44].
- Smart specialization and sport sampling (John O'Sullivan, Changing the Game Project, is cited on athlete engagement) [21:18] [21:48].
- Youth basketball is named as an example of a sport adopting this approach, with lacrosse and tennis also mentioned; another speaker ("Dr. D Fury", caption spelling) is referenced [21:48] [22:18].

## Limits and open questions

- Almost no sample sizes or effect sizes are given; the specialization and NBA findings are stated briefly without sources.
- The complex-systems model is described as the speaker's own hypothesis [17:15] and she says it is unclear whether 10,000 hours, intrinsic ability or load quality drives elite performance [14:40].
- The recommendation to play multiple sports collides with ranking and selection of ten-year-olds, which the speaker names but does not resolve [12:59].
- Population-level youth framing; no measures or thresholds for individual athletes are offered.

# SSAC19: Performance Optimization Strategies that Helped Win a Championship

## Summary

The West Coast Eagles' high performance manager describes four guiding principles and four "big rocks" that he credits with preparing the club for its 2018 Grand Final win. The principles are levels of perspective, the Hedgehog principle, start with why, and big rocks before small marginal gains. The big rocks are a strategic plan with objectives and key results, having the best players available, a high chronic running load, and training that matches or exceeds the hardest running in a game. The evidence is one club's data presented by its own staff, and the talk is sponsored by a data platform vendor.

## Key claims

- The speaker's department has medical, strength and conditioning, and sports science branches, with a research arm that always has a student working on a club question [05:39].
- Single events such as one hamstring or ACL are not worried over; a run of events signals the systems and structures are not working [06:40].
- Doing one or two things very well (the Hedgehog principle, from Jim Collins's work) and documenting the reason behind each plan (start with why) guide decisions [07:11] [07:41] [08:43].
- Teams are distracted by small one-percent gains; the big rocks should be placed first, and sand added after [09:14]. The example given is altitude camps for a small aerobic gain while kicking effectiveness stayed poor; he would rather fund kicking coaches [09:44] [10:15].
- Big rock one: a strategic plan following vision, mission, objectives, strategies and tactics, with key results per objective, which aligns all staff and is described as a competitive advantage [10:45] [11:15].
- Big rock two: get the best players on the field. The club's data led it to target nine or more of its top 10 players each week [12:18] [12:49].
- Few clubs can field their best players often; the club exceeded the league average for this last season [13:20] [13:52].
- A star young player's development is shown with official provider points to argue best players must play [14:23] [14:53].
- Big rock three: chronic load, defined as a rolling four-week average of work done; high chronic load is needed so that game spikes are not excessive [15:55] [16:26] [16:57].
- A mandated two-week Christmas break drops chronic load enough that returning to the same session lands in very high risk, so players must train in off periods [17:58] [18:30].
- Big rock four: hard running. Being fit does not mean being conditioned, so the club identified the hardest 15 minutes of running in five years and built drills matching or exceeding it, with a belief effect on players [19:02] [19:33] [20:06] [20:38].
- Message: align staff and coaches with one plan, put big rocks before one-percenters, ignore what other clubs or one paper do, and keep data simple but not simpler [21:39] [22:10].

## Numbers and definitions

- Collins study: over 1,400 companies, 11 that made the leap from good to great [07:11].
- Altitude trip: 200,000 to 300,000 dollars, 2 percent gain in aerobic capacity, about 50 percent kicking effectiveness; he would prefer to spend 400,000 dollars on two kicking coaches [09:44] [10:15].
- Example key result: no more than 15 percent of injuries should be recurrences of a previous injury [11:46].
- Top-10 availability objective: nine or more of the top 10 each week [12:18]. With all 10, win rate 80 percent (four of five); with nine, two-thirds [12:49].
- League average: 10 of 10 available only 15 percent of the time, nine of 10 about 25 percent (the caption mentions 18 as the competition's club count) [13:20].
- Club season: average 8.7 of 10 over 25 games, nine or more on 15 occasions [14:53]. Eight of 10 by season end and seven in the Grand Final [15:24].
- Chronic load: rolling four-week average [15:55]. Risk bands: green "sweet spot", pink two times risk, dark red three to five times risk [17:27].
- Weekly running about 30 km plus, tackled about 10 times (caption wording) [16:26].
- Midfielder covers 15 to 16 km in a game; hardest block was one midfielder running about 180 m per minute on a rolling five-minute average over the first 15 minutes [18:30] [19:33].
- Field 170 m long by 130 m wide [20:06].
- Drills at the hardest running duration: four occasions of 12 minutes or more, the captions for the 9-to-12 and 6-to-9 minute counts are garbled (eight times each is the likeliest reading) [21:08].

## Methods and frameworks named

- Levels of perspective (Daniel Kim) [06:09].
- Hedgehog principle (Jim Collins) [07:11].
- Start with why (Simon Sinek, caption spelling "Simon syic") [08:43].
- Big rocks metaphor [09:14].

## Limits and open questions

- One club, one season, with the club's own staff reporting outcomes; no control or comparison is shown for the load and drill choices.
- Source and sample for the risk bands (two times, three to five times) are not given.
- The speaker says other research links squad-wide injury count to performance but his club's data points to the best players mattering [12:18].
- The Grand Final win is not attributed to a tested cause; he lists things they did.
- Two caption problems: the opposition's count of available top players is cut off [15:55], and the drill duration counts are garbled [21:08].
- The talk is sponsored by Fusion Sport and the speaker praises their platform [01:06] [22:42].

## Q&A

- Can cycling-style performance modeling be used? The game is too chaotic and random, fields vary, so the club models only a little in training [23:14] [23:47] [24:17].
- Biggest marginal gain? The mental side; the club has a part-time performance psychologist and added mindfulness before meetings [24:59] [25:30].
- How is load tracked when players are away? Players log their program in the platform, and the staff manage the group whose chronic load dropped [26:08].
- Data over time? Long, clean data allows slow increases in group load across years while staying in the sweet spot [26:41] [27:12].
